analysis.one_liner: Caps interest on most consumer loans at 36% APR, extending protections now given to service members to everyone.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it was referred to the Senate Banking Committee in December 2023 and sat there until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Military service members and their families are already protected from loans that charge more than 36% annual interest under the Military Lending Act. This bill would give that same protection to all consumers, capping the interest rate on consumer credit — including payday loans, installment loans, and credit cards — at 36% APR. Mortgages, car purchase loans, and federal credit union loans would be exempt, and states could keep stronger rules of their own. The bill was introduced on the last weeks of the 2023 session and never advanced out of the Senate Banking Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Borrowers who today pay triple-digit rates on payday, title, and installment loans, and cardholders who pay rates above 36% plus add-on fees, would see the cost of borrowing capped. Research on the military version of this cap has shown service members kept access to credit after it took effect.

how_it_helps.text: The bill applies the Military Lending Act's core protections — including its 36% rate cap — to every consumer, not just service members and their dependents.

It bans the CFPB from granting exemptions to the new cap, and it defines the annual percentage rate for open-end credit using the Defense Department's finance-charge rules, so lenders cannot shift costs into fees.
It keeps state laws that are stricter than the federal cap fully intact, and lets state attorneys general and state regulators sue violators for three years after a violation.
Credit insurance premiums, debt-cancellation fees, and other credit-related add-on products are not exempted from the finance-charge calculation, closing a common loophole in high-cost card lending.

analysis.who_pays: Lenders whose business model depends on rates above 36% — payday, title, and installment lenders and issuers of high-fee subprime cards — would lose the revenue those loans generate. Some borrowers with poor credit might find fewer lenders willing to serve them at the capped rate.
analysis.who_pays_short: High-cost lenders and subprime card issuers

drawbacks.text: The strongest good-faith objection is that a hard rate cap can cut off credit: lenders say they cannot profitably serve high-risk borrowers at 36%, so some people may lose access to emergency credit entirely rather than get cheaper credit.

The bill's cost falls entirely on lenders that currently charge more than 36%, so firms in that business would shrink or exit — a real cost to the industry and potentially to some borrowers' access to small-dollar loans.
Enforcement depends on CFPB rules and on state attorneys general and regulators suing within a three-year window, so under-enforcement could blunt the cap's effect.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to ordinary borrowers is large and concrete: a 36% APR ceiling on most consumer credit, with no agency discretion to waive it and state enforcement preserved. The honest cost is that a national cap of this level would eliminate much of today's payday, title, and subprime credit market, and some high-risk borrowers could be left with fewer options. Evidence from the existing military cap suggests credit did not disappear for covered borrowers, which is the strongest argument the trade is worth it.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Banking Committee, which never took it up, and it died there when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Jack Reed introduced the bill on December 14, 2023, with 16 Senate Democratic cosponsors, and it was read twice and referred to the Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee.
The action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action — the bill's only recorded Senate action is the referral itself.
The Congress ended on January 3, 2025, so the bill expired without ever receiving a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Lenders that charge more than 36% — payday, title, and installment lenders and high-fee card issuers — are better off, because the rate cap never advanced far enough to threaten their business.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High-cost lenders, since the bill died

for.name: Sen. Jack Reed
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Predatory Lending Elimination Act to extend the Military Lending Act's 36% rate cap to all consumers.

for.name: 17 Senate Democrats
for.role: Cosponsors, including Sherrod Brown, Elizabeth Warren-era Banking Chair Brown (D-OH), Jeff Merkley, and Richard Blumenthal
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors at introduction.

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.role: Committee of referral in the 118th Congress
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never held a markup or reported it out, keeping it from reaching the Senate floor.

against.name: High-cost lending industry
against.role: Payday, title, installment, and subprime credit card lenders
against.what_they_did: The industry has long opposed national rate caps, which would eliminate most of its lending above 36% APR; no such opposition appears in this bill's congressional record.

sides.party_line_note: All 18 Senate supporters were Democrats — the sponsor and 17 cosponsors — with no Republican cosponsor, and the bill never reached a vote where any partisan split would have been recorded.

industries.note: These lenders' business depends on rates far above 36%; a universal cap that has applied to the military since 2006 would eliminate most of their lending. Ordinary borrowers would pay far less but could lose access to this credit.

industries.industry: Credit card issuers and subprime consumer lenders
industries.note: Cards charging above 36% APR, and add-on products like credit insurance, would be barred under the bill's finance-charge rules. Most prime-rate cards would be unaffected.

Loans from federal credit unions, which already operate under a statutory 18% rate limit, are explicitly exempted from the bill's cap, leaving them free to serve small-dollar borrowers the bill prices out of the market.
